newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr creeps ahead as yields shift its way.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr creeps ahead as yields shift its way.

text.p: The Australian dollar made modest gains Wednesday but failed to live up to early promise.

It had started strongly after benign U.S. wages data made the market rein back its expectations for the likely extent of the U.S. tightening cycle. Japanese buying of AUD/yen related to a couple of dual currency samurai issues then saw it threaten US$0.7830 resistance, a two-week high for the currency.

But the bullishness proved brief as sellers engulfed it, reinforcing recent rumours of huge offers lurking in this area. Nevertheless, the resulting pullback was shallow leading dealers to expect at least one more tilt at the upside tonight.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the unit was still making threatening jestures at US$0.7813/18 having been unable to sustain the push from an early early US$0.7816/21.
That was ahead of Tuesday's late US$0.7790/95 and its first local finish atop 78 cents since April 14.
Chart watchers were sceptical it could break higher given the strength of resistance but had pencilled in targets of US$0.7860 and US$0.7890 just in case.
On the downside, the loss of US$0.7770 would point to more sideways drift ahead and put US$0.7720 at risk, although dealers felt the re-emergence of Japanese demand should prevent this.
Japanese funds had been big buyers of Australian government bonds recently and were joined by retail investors today as a couple of dual currency samurai issues were launched.
The largest came from Western Australia Treasury Corp which issued a 40 bln yen bond with redemption in A$.
The currency climbed as high as 99.35 in response and was holding firm at 99.15/25 at the close from Tuesday's late 98.67/77. In trade weighted terms it was up 0.1 point at 60.7.
The burst of Japanese demand partly reflected a sharp slide in U.S. yields Tuesday which had seen interest differentials and swap spreads shift in the local dollar's favour.
The fall in U.S. market rates came after a key measure of U.S. labour costs proved much softer than expected in Q1.

Analysts were not certain this alone would prevent the Federal Reserve from tightening at its May 20 meeting, but it did suggest the ultimate amount of tightening needed would be less than previously thought.

That was bullish for the local dollar which had been in danger of seeing U.S. official rates surpass those here for the first time since the early 1980s. But there was yet a chance the Reserve Bank would decide to take further insurance out on the domestic recovery by easing Australian rates.
Domestic trade data today, while not directly relevant to monetary policy, did suggest domestic demand was muted in March and exports could be under pressure from the strong dollar.

The balance of goods and services swung to a A$103 million deficit in March when a surplus of A$150 million had been expected. Exports slid nine percent while total imports fell five percent and consumption goods imports fell seven percent.

Analysts emphasised it was difficult to draw conclusions from the volatile monthly trade data, but were interested to see if the softness in consumption imports was reflected in the retail sales data for March on Friday.
More vital for the rate outlook should be average weekly earnings data for Q1 due Thursday which are expected to show some increase in wages growth.
Elsewhere, recent speculation about the impending sale of three Federal airports was confirmed by Finance Minister John Fahey who said the government was close to a decision.

Rumour has valued the sale price as high as A$3.0 billion and, since the main bidding consortia include a large foreign presence, implies a possible net offshore need to buy A$ to pay for the airports.
